sections.heading: 1. Sound and its Propagation
points: **Sound is produced by vibrating objects** and travels as a **wave**.
Sound is a **longitudinal wave** — particles of the medium vibrate **back and forth along** the direction of travel, creating **compressions and rarefactions**.
Sound **needs a material medium** (solid/liquid/gas) — it **cannot travel through vacuum**; it travels **fastest in solids**, slowest in gases.

sections.heading: 2. Characteristics of a Sound Wave
points: **Frequency (f)** — vibrations per second (**hertz, Hz**); decides **pitch**.
**Amplitude** — decides **loudness**.
**Wavelength (λ)** — distance between two consecutive compressions/rarefactions.
**Speed = frequency × wavelength (v = fλ)**; **time period = 1/frequency**.
**Audible range** = **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**; below = **infrasound**, above = **ultrasound**.

sections.heading: 3. Reflection of Sound — Echo and Reverberation
points: **Reflection of sound** obeys the laws of reflection.
**Echo** = a reflected sound heard distinctly; needs the reflecting surface to be **≥ ~17.2 m** away (so the reflected sound arrives after 0.1 s).
**Reverberation** = repeated reflections making sound persist (in halls) — reduced by sound-absorbing materials.
Uses: **megaphone, stethoscope, sound in auditoriums (curved ceilings)**.

sections.heading: 4. Applications — Ultrasound and SONAR
points: **Ultrasound** (>20,000 Hz) is used in **medicine (ultrasonography/scans)**, cleaning, detecting cracks in metals.
**SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging)** uses ultrasound to find the **depth of the sea** and locate objects (submarines, shoals) using **echo (echo-ranging)**.
Bats and dolphins use ultrasound to navigate (**echolocation**).

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Sound = longitudinal wave (compressions & rarefactions); needs a medium (no sound in vacuum); fastest in solids.
Frequency (Hz) → pitch; amplitude → loudness; v = fλ.
Audible range = 20–20,000 Hz; below = infrasound, above = ultrasound.
Echo needs the surface ≥ ~17.2 m away; reverberation = repeated reflections.
SONAR uses ultrasound + echo to measure sea depth; bats use echolocation.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: Sound is a **longitudinal** wave and **cannot travel through vacuum**.
**Pitch depends on frequency**; **loudness on amplitude**.
For an **echo**, the reflecting surface must be at least about **17.2 m** away.
**SONAR** uses **ultrasound** and the principle of **echo (echo-ranging)**.
